$comment: Conformance traceability manifest (#245). Each requirement row maps one normative clause (or one facet of a multi-part clause) to its observable conformance assertion and the tests that drive it. Validated by scripts/check-conformance-manifest.mjs: unknown anchors, quoted clauses missing from their anchored section, duplicate IDs, missing tests, and coverage states inconsistent with their mappings all fail CI; rows not fully tested are the visible outstanding report, never silent. observation.local records this implementation's chosen behavior where the spec permits more than one; a local pin never becomes the protocol requirement. Rows whose applicability names a capability, or all of several (kind capabilities, member all_of), apply only where the deployment claims each one: a runner MUST NOT mark an unclaimed capability nonconforming, and a failed SHOULD row is a recorded departure, not a hard fail. source.specs names, for every spec file a row references, the revision (the commit whose text that spec's rows were validated against) and content_sha256 (a mechanical gate recomputed from the working-tree file's current bytes, which must match, or the entry needs deliberate re-review and a bump before CI passes again); the stale-text check catches an edited or relocated clause inside an anchored section, source.specs catches any other edit to a spec whose rows were not re-reviewed. Completeness provenance per spec lives in the tracking issues, not in this manifest. Each row's profiles array (enumerated at the top level in profiles) names which published baseline profile(s) this requirement belongs to: a floor document beyond core typically carries only runtime-enforced, core typically carries both, and an empty array means this requirement belongs to no published baseline profile, whether because its document sits outside every baseline or because a baseline document's own row is scoped to an optional capability no published baseline selects; profiles and applicability are orthogonal, since applicability already encodes election of an OPTIONAL capability.

requirements.text: A claiming deployment MUST publish the covered classes and operations, each operation's versioned binding descriptor, and whether it reaches the verified or enforced property below.

observation.normative: a deployment claiming the extension publishes the covered classes and operations, each operation's versioned binding descriptor, and which of the verified or enforced property it reaches

the Evaluation-Context Binding declaration is refused at load unless complete (@spec runtime#evaluation-context-binding, #773) > a claiming class without an operation, a descriptor or a resolver is refused at load

the shipped declaration and the Operation Profile agree (@spec runtime#evaluation-context-binding, #773) > every crossing of a covered class is a covered operation, and every covered crossing captures under the shipped descriptors

requirements.notes: #773. The shipped statement claims the extension and publishes extensions.evaluation_context_binding: covered classes irreversible_action and external_commitment, the covered operations (payments:payment.execute with its preflight, prepare and commit crossings, payments:remittance.send, and payments:payment.reverse at its compensate crossing, #252), each operation's descriptor reference, and the verified property; the loader refuses a claim lacking a declaration, an operation, a covered class's operation, a descriptor or a fact's resolver. The PEP-side test checks the profile and the published declaration agree. Mutations: publishing enforced with a declared precondition fails the admission test (C3); dropping the loader's findings (L20) or the covered-class check (L25) fails the refusal test; uncovering the commit crossing fails the agreement test (C1).

observation.normative: re-resolving a published `{id, version}` reference returns byte-identical descriptor content whose digest still equals the reference's `digest`; a revised descriptor is published under a new version rather than replacing those bytes

requirements.notes: #773. Each declared descriptor document is hashed at load and one that no longer hashes to its reference is refused, claimed or not (L23), and the PEP re-hashes the document when it resolves a reference; a revised descriptor is published under a new version, whose different reference changes the committed digest over the same facts (the composition test). Mutations: L23 fails the load test; M5 fails the composition test.

requirements.notes: #773. The committed object is reconstructed member for member (descriptor reference, Mission, operation and phase, targets, facts, salt and version) and its canonical-object digest equals the one sent; a republished descriptor over unchanged facts commits a different digest at capture. A permit decided under the earlier reference is never reinterpreted: at use the context is recomputed under the committed reference (so unchanged facts give an equal digest) and the descriptor change is refused on its own, target_drift. Mutations: M5 (reference not committed) fails the composition test; X1 (recompute under the live descriptor) and X2 (descriptor-change check removed) fail the changed-descriptor test.

requirements.notes: #773. The PEP resolves every declared fact from the payments store records the request's invoice names: arguments naming the authoritative facts (amount, payee_account, invoice_version) do not change the captured digest, while a change to the store's record does; the composition test shows the committed facts are the store's values. Mutation M6 (an argument entering the commitment) fails the first. #252: the compensate crossing's authoritative interface is the committed wire's ledger record: an invoice changed after its wire committed, and again before release, leaves the captured context equal to one computed from the wire's record, and the reversal offsets the wire's USD 125. Mutation C1 (the compensate crossing's facts read from the live invoice) fails it; S1 (a resolver reading a record other than its own) fails the shipped-agreement test, which also shows the compensate descriptor's facts do not resolve from the invoice. Each resolver names the crossings it serves: the compensate crossing reads its effect facts only from the wire record and from the store only the live facts its decision evaluates, so a descriptor naming the invoice's amount for it does not capture (S2, the restriction removed, fails that test; L4, the live facts withheld from the compensate crossing, fails every compensate test). #1663 review 3: the compensating decision's live properties and its context capture are built from one synchronous observation of the store records, taken after the link's awaits: a tenant, issuance or classification moved during the awaited verification of the link's evidence reaches the request as moved, the PDP's bound denies at the decision, and the committed context is that same observation. Mutations: R1 (the live properties read before the awaits) and R1b (that plus the capture re-reading the store) fail all three; R2 (the capture re-reading the store right after the snapshot) survives, as an equivalent mutation: no await separates the two reads, which is the property the single snapshot guarantees. #1693 (D873): the compensate crossing's tenant fact is the current tenant of the vendor the committed wire paid, read by the wire's vendor in the decision snapshot and at release, never the vendor the invoice names now (resolver payments-store:paid-vendor.tenant, which serves only the compensate crossing; descriptor payment-reverse version 2026-10-26). After the invoice moves from the paid vendor to another, the decision request carries the paid vendor and its tenant: a bound naming that tenant permits and the reversal offsets the paid vendor's wire, and one naming the new vendor's tenant is denied at the decision. An invoice reassigned between the decision and release still releases, its context re-established equal. A paid vendor gone before the decision is refused unknown_vendor with no decision request, though the invoice's current vendor resolves. A capture reads the paid vendor from the store and does not resolve handed-in records naming another vendor (target_unresolvable), and payments-store:vendor.tenant (the tenant of the vendor an invoice names) does not serve the compensate crossing. Mutations: PV1 (the snapshot reads the invoice's current vendor) fails the moved-invoice and gone-before-decision witnesses (the vendor-id check refuses the capture evaluation_context_unresolvable; with PV3 as well, the decision evaluates the new vendor's tenant and the paid vendor's bound is denied); PV2 (the recompute reads the invoice's current vendor) fails the moved-invoice, reassigned-before-release and store-read witnesses, as does PV2 with PV3; PV3 (the vendor-id check on handed-in records removed) fails the records witness, the only one that can reach it, since the PEP hands in only the paid vendor's record; PV4 (payments-store:vendor.tenant serving the compensate crossing) fails the resolver witness. D879: with the invoice's current vendor deleted after it moved, the reversal's context is captured from the invoice and the paid vendor and re-established equal at release (I1 fails it).

requirements.text: Adoption MUST preserve existing approval-to-decision, transaction-token, parameter, and operation-idempotency bindings.

observation.normative: adopting the extension leaves the approval-to-decision, transaction-token, parameter, and operation-idempotency bindings intact, so no earlier approval or operation identity authorizes changed effect parameters

tests.name: claim applicability: covered, uncovered and non-claiming (@spec runtime#evaluation-context-binding, authzen#response-context, #773) > the parameter digest, the operation key and so the approval and transaction-token bindings are unchanged by the claim

adoption keeps the approval and transaction-token bindings (@spec runtime#evaluation-context-binding, #773) > an action-bound approval bound to parameter_digest satisfies the gate under the claim, and stops satisfying it once the record moves before the decision

adoption keeps the approval and transaction-token bindings (@spec runtime#evaluation-context-binding, #773) > a transaction token bound to the challenged operation's parameter_digest verifies and executes once under the claim

adoption keeps the approval and transaction-token bindings (@spec runtime#evaluation-context-binding, #773) > a transaction token issued before the record moved is refused under the claim, with no effect

requirements.notes: #773, additive binding. Each clause is witnessed under the claim. Parameter and operation-idempotency: the claimed and unclaimed deployments send byte-identical parameter_digest and derive the same operation key (M30, a covered crossing's digest dropping the facts the context binds, fails it). Approval-to-decision: an action-bound approval bound to parameter_digest satisfies the wire's approval gate beside the context members, and once the record moves before the decision the same approval no longer does (M30 fails the first half; disabling the PDP's approval digest comparison fails the second). Transaction token: a token bound to the challenged operation's digest verifies and executes once, and one issued before the record moved is refused txn_parameter_mismatch with no effect (M30 fails the first; skipping the token's parameter recomputation fails the second, whose zero-effect assertion also fails alone). So no earlier approval or operation identity authorizes changed effect parameters after a fresh context capture.

requirements.notes: #773 ruling 1. Per-epoch salt: each version is in-memory random material under a random identifier, so a restarted keeper holds none of an earlier one's versions and the binding is never recomputed under a substitute; it is refused target_drift with the effective context digest absent on every covered dispatch path. A committed descriptor the declaration no longer publishes is the same refusal, with no comparison under the live descriptor (X3). Mutations: M4 (recompute under the current salt) fails the absent-digest assertion of all four restart tests and the unrecoverable test; removing the context check at use (M1+M2) fails them outright. Zero effects: committedEffects() is the zero-effect witness on the transaction path only; on the read and write paths it is the refused call, which returns no result.

requirements.notes: #773. A covered permit's conditions.evaluation_context_digest is the request's digest echoed verbatim, an arbitrary well-formed value the PDP could not compute without the PEP's salt, over the in-process and remote paths; the signed record carries no salt. Facts stay available to policy: with the same valid context inputs, an amount over the entry's cap, an absent amount and a vendor outside the entry are each denied parameter_violation, while the in-cap request permits and queries Resource policy. The remote test is titled for the refusal; its second half serves a well-formed request and asserts the echoed condition. Mutations: P14 (no echo) fails the remote echo assertion cleanly and trips the emitter's equality guard in process; F2 (the amount cap skipped when a context binding is established) fails the facts test.

requirements.notes: #773. Each clause refuses before any effect: a permit lacking the condition (M9); a changed descriptor, refused by its own check with the context recomputed under the committed descriptor and equal (X2, M1+M2); an unequal digest after a moved fact (M2); and an unavailable fact while the parameters still resolve (M1+M2 turns it into parameter_mismatch) or an unrecoverable salt or committed descriptor (M4, X3, M1+M2). Zero effects: committedEffects() is the zero-effect witness on the transaction path only; on the read and write paths it is the refused call, which returns no result. #252: on the compensate crossing, a moved fact of the committed wire's record (C2 turns it into parameter_mismatch) and a record that no longer answers (C1 leaves an effective context digest) each refuse before any reversal. #252 owner review of #1663: the compensating decision also evaluates live resource facts (the invoice's issuance and classification and the current tenant of the vendor the committed wire paid (#1693), through the Common Constraints), so the compensate descriptor declares them beside the committed wire's effect facts. A reversal approved under a tenant, issuance or classification bound whose fact moves before release is refused target_drift with zero effects, the wire's parameter pair equal and the context pair unequal. Mutations: L1, L2 and L3 (each live fact frozen) each fail its test; M1+C2 (no context check at the compensate crossing's use) fails all three. #1663 review 3, ruling 3: an invoice or vendor record removed between the decision and release on the compensate crossing is target_drift with zero reversal entries, the wire's parameter pair kept and the effective context digest absent (M1+C2 and D2, an unestablishable context classified parameter_mismatch, each fail both). #1693 (D873): with the invoice moved to another vendor, the paid vendor's tenant moved after the decision is target_drift with zero reversal entries, the wire's parameter pair equal and the context pair unequal, and the paid vendor's record removed after the decision is target_drift with zero reversal entries and no effective context digest. Mutations: PV1 fails both; PV2 with PV3 (the recompute reads and accepts the invoice's current vendor) fails the removal witness, which then records an effective context digest.

requirements.notes: #773 ruling 5. Each crossing of payments:payment.execute captures its own context with its own phase committed (one parameter digest, three context digests) and is checked at its own use on its own dispatch path (read, write, transaction), as is payments:remittance.send; a commit permit carrying the prepare crossing's context binding is refused. partial only for the prepare-stable SHOULD: no shipped descriptor declares a prepare-stable fact (the descriptor reader refuses any member it does not implement, so none can be declared), so that branch is inapplicable to the shipped claim and is not implemented. Mutations: M23 (phase not committed) fails the distinct-digest and prepare-on-commit tests; M1 fails the read-path test and M2 the write and transaction tests. Zero effects: committedEffects() is the zero-effect witness on the transaction path only; on the read and write paths it is the refused call, which returns no result. #252: the compensate crossing of payments:payment.reverse captures its own context under its own descriptor, after its link to the committed wire is established, and is checked at its own use; mutations C3 (no capture there), C4 (its fresh parameters re-derived from the invoice) and C5 (recomputation ignoring the committed wire) each fail that test. The compensate crossing's context also covers the live facts its own decision evaluates (L1 fails the tenant witness); its tenant fact is the current tenant of the vendor the committed wire paid (#1693, witnessed under runtime.evaluation-context.capture-authoritative). #1663 review 3: the compensating decision's live properties and its context capture are built from one synchronous observation of the store records, taken after the link's awaits: a tenant, issuance or classification moved during the awaited verification of the link's evidence reaches the request as moved, the PDP's bound denies at the decision, and the committed context is that same observation. Mutations: R1 (the live properties read before the awaits) and R1b (that plus the capture re-reading the store) fail all three; R2 (the capture re-reading the store right after the snapshot) survives, as an equivalent mutation: no await separates the two reads, which is the property the single snapshot guarantees.

requirements.text: The **enforced** property MUST NOT be claimed without an atomic resource-side comparison coupled to the effect.

requirements.notes: #773. The completed record of every covered crossing carries the effective context digest: the write paths pass the digest reverification re-established before the effect, the read path's disposition writer re-establishes it now, and the transaction tier's completed record carries reverification's. A completed disposition that cannot re-establish it is the reported gap effective_evaluation_context_digest_unobservable, the counterpart of #786's effective_parameter_digest_unobservable, never a record that drops the member. Under a changed descriptor the digest is computed under the retained original. Mutations: E1 (the disposition writer drops the effective member on a completed record) fails the check_transfer and hold_transfer completed tests; E2 (the gap removed, so the record is emitted without the member) fails the gap test; X1 (recomputed under the live descriptor) fails the retained-original tests. requirements.notes: #252 PR C2 (owner rulings 2026-10-24, D762). The compensate crossing reverse_wire_transfer (payments:payment.reverse) offsets a wire execute_wire_transfer committed, through the reference ledger connector, under its own single-use compensate Decision whose signed Decision Evidence carries compensates_evaluation_id equal to the commit's evaluation_id; the reversal entry names the wire's operation key and the compensation's own permit, the wire entry is unchanged, and reconciliation joins both effects to completed Execution Evidence. The PEP establishes the link from its own retained records, which it re-verifies, never from an argument: an argument naming another evaluation is not read past the tool boundary and is refused at intake on it. In the composed stack the records re-verify through the boundary-bound resolver and the link reaches the PDP, whose denial records it. Mutations: recording another value as the link fails the Decision Evidence assertion; a reversal that inserts nothing fails the connector assertion; reconciliation without reversal entries fails the reconcile assertion; a request carrying another link, or the agent-supplied one, fails the envelope assertion; a stack resolver without the executor's key fails the stack's verification assertion. A simulated connector establishes reference behavior, not real bank reversal semantics. Owner review of PR #1656: the compensating Decision binds the committed wire's own parameters (the reversal form read from the wire's ledger record), and the offset is exactly the committed amount even after the invoice changed; its Decision Evidence and Execution Evidence carry that form's digest.

requirements.notes: Owner review of PR #1656 (P1). Committing USD 125, changing the invoice to USD 1 and requesting a reversal under a USD 10 reversal ceiling is denied parameter_violation, the request carrying USD 125, with zero connector effects; within the ceiling the reversal offsets exactly USD 125, and the request, Decision Evidence, operation key and completed Execution Evidence carry the digest of the wire's reversal form; a wire record that changes after the Decision is refused at use: target_drift under the shipped Evaluation-Context Binding claim, which covers the compensate crossing and declares the wire's amount a fact (#773), and parameter_mismatch in a deployment that does not claim it. Mutations: binding the invoice as it reads now fails the denial assertion (the permit is then refused at use); doing so with the at-use comparison and the connector check also off reverses USD 125 (the zero-effect assertion fails on its own); binding the current amount into the reversal form with both downstream guards off fails the committed-amount assertion; skipping the at-use comparison fails the non-claiming at-use witness (U1, #773: under the shipped claim the context check refuses the changed record first, so that witness no longer isolates the comparison). After #786: a wire record that no longer answers at use leaves the effective parameters unestablished, suppressed target_drift with the authorized digest kept and the effective one absent. Mutation: recording that case as parameter_mismatch fails the target_drift witness. #773: binding the compensate crossing's live resource facts does not move its effect parameters: an invoice amount changed after the wire, and again before release, still reverses the wire's USD 125 under the parameter digest the Decision bound (P1, the reversal's amount taken from the invoice, fails that witness too). #1693 (D873): after the invoice moves from the vendor its wire paid to another, the compensating decision request still carries the wire's vendor, with that vendor's current tenant, and the reversal offsets the paid vendor's wire under a bound naming that tenant, with or without the Evaluation-Context Binding claim; a bound naming the new vendor's tenant is denied at the decision. Mutations: PV5 (the decision's vendor_id taken from the invoice as it reads now) and PV6 (the reversal form's vendor_id taken from it) each fail both. D879: the compensate crossing never reads the vendor the invoice names now. With the invoice moved to another vendor whose record is then deleted, the reversal still carries the wire's vendor and that vendor's current tenant, permits under a bound on that tenant and offsets the paid vendor's wire, with or without the Evaluation-Context Binding claim; an ordinary invoice-scoped operation still refuses that missing vendor unknown_vendor before any decision request. Mutation I1 (the generic unknown_vendor requirement restored on the compensate path) fails both. D889: the transaction-token retry of a challenged reversal recomputes the same reversal form from the committed effect's retained record, so the approved retry releases one reversal of the paid wire, also when the invoice was reassigned to a vendor deleted between the challenge and the retry. Mutation A1 (the invoice form on the retry path) fails both.

requirements.notes: #1535 (D649, finding 2). Partial (#1543 review): of the reference's two consumer paths, only the resolver enforces every term. The resolver (the PDP's own read) is tested on all three: fresh_until, the advertised ceiling (iat plus mission_max_stale_seconds) and, through check 10, exp; the separated pilot caps its permit at the resulting bound (the wiring test). The PEP-carried `assertion` path in evaluate.ts cannot enforce the advertised ceiling: it holds no issuer metadata, and only the action class's staleness window bounds the observation's age there. That path is tested on fresh_until (the two evaluate tests) and, through check 10, on exp. requirements.notes: Single-process fault coverage: conditional state/version and counter writes admitted from the stored row, rollback-safe nested publication, child fanout admission in the creation transaction, expansion deferral retirement with successor and supersession, and lifecycle state/version with durable publication work and the terminal tombstone in one transaction. The counter now carries a durable operation and artifact identity: the increment and its reservation commit together, a recorded operation identity replays its artifact instead of counting again, an unreleased reservation is never refunded because a missing local acknowledgement is not evidence that no artifact was accepted, and only an authoritative non-acceptance returns a count. A refunded operation identity is terminal and refuses a retry, so nothing issues against a count that was returned; and a pending reservation is exclusive on this instance, so two overlapping callers under one operation identity receive one artifact rather than two against one count. The lifecycle nonce claim and its committed outcome now commit with the transition, with the exact response finalized and recovered outside that transaction, and finalization is guarded on the request digest the claim was made under so a divergent retry can neither overwrite a committed success nor be retained in its place. The expiry clock commits in its own transaction ahead of the requested transition, so refusing that transition never rolls back the expiry it discovered or the expiry's publication. A request's `expected_version` is compared with the version that expiry left, so a caller's earlier version is refused `stale_version` while the expiry stays committed and published once (#250). That claim store's additive schema migration is exercised on a file-backed database carrying the pre-migration shape: every retained outcome keeps its replay identity, and a reopen is a no-op. The continuation anchors and handles and the delegation families are kernel tables written in the committing transaction: the activating commit roots a Mission's lineage with its record, the terminal commit terminates its lineages beside the tombstone, an activation replayed after the Mission terminated roots nothing, and on the file-backed kernel they survive a restart (#250). This does not reach tested in this slice: the artifact itself is still issued outside the kernel transaction (the provider access-token hook is synchronous and has no acceptance boundary), so authoritative issuance state and artifact material are not recorded transactionally before delivery. No multi-process claim.

requirements.text: A signer of a state observation MUST NOT manufacture freshness by assigning a new `iat` or `fresh_until` to an older observation without establishing that its value reflects the authoritative committed state at the new observation point.

observation.normative: A signer of a state observation MUST NOT manufacture freshness by assigning a new `iat` or `fresh_until` to an older observation without establishing that its value reflects the authoritative committed state at the new observation point. The issuer establishes an authenticated observation/commit watermark justified by its consistency mechanism. An authoritative transactional read, quorum/read-index, or correctly defined lease mechanism can provide that guarantee; a lease alone does not prove inclusion of a committed transition. Without it, the signer may replay an original authenticated snapshot only within that snapshot's original validity and audience binding, or refuse. Signature validity proves producer and integrity, not recency. The Status freshness ceiling is unchanged.

requirements.notes: The signed-artifact inventory in src/docs/control-plane-deployment.md classifies every signed artifact the reference produces (#1750). Three are state observations, each witnessed with a mutation that re-dates it. The Mission Status response is taken in one authoritative transactional read that carries its (version, commit) watermark, and its iat, exp and fresh_until belong to that read, never to the clock at signature time; a commit during the signature leaves it older, not re-dated. Lifecycle responses: a recovered response is signed over the recorded observation with its original iat, exp and fresh_until, and a retained envelope replays its exact bytes for the nonce window, past its own validity, solely as confirmation of the correlated original operation with every other check passing: it refreshes no state and authorizes nothing, and it is not a general exception that holding a watermark confers. The Mission Status List publisher serves a token only inside its own validity, rebuilds from the record set rather than re-signing cached bits, and lets no older in-flight snapshot land after a newer commit. A Mission Signals SET is a transition record (D993): its observation point is the committed_at recorded at commit, its iat is RFC 8417 issuance time, and a SET first signed hours after its commit keeps that committed_at; the receiver orders by version, never iat. The Join Assertion is an attestation with no state, version or fresh_until, whose cache replays original bytes only inside its exp and audience binding. Credentials take iat as issuance time, not a statement of current state: the AS's Mission-bound OAuth access tokens, ID-JAGs and AAT roots are gated on Mission state at mint with exp bounded by the Mission's expiry, while a holder-minted offline AAT child and an ARAP approval (bounded by approved_until, with no JWT exp) check no Mission state, and no mint-time state claim is made for the other credentials; records carry their recorded event times. The Status freshness ceiling is witnessed by the cap tests. Refusing an observation whose commit point advanced is a declared optional policy, off; its defects (it blocks Lifecycle response recovery, and its commit member falls after boot pruning) are #1865, availability under that option, not freshness. No current Status draft specifies a conditional-request surface, so none is owed (D874).

observation.local: the Signals receiver's lease (#1747) gives no lease while the rematerialization latch or a version gap is open, or once an active state's reliance bound has passed, and reports the issuer's observation time and bound unchanged at every read; Mission Status (resynchronize, under a nonce from statusNonce) re-establishes the state: a response below the stored version is refused whatever its state, one at the stored version refreshes the observation time and bound and clears the gap, and one above it replaces the state, a higher-version active over a stored suspended included. A Status refresh never clears the rematerialization latch, since a state-only response carries no effective authority: the consumer acknowledges it (markRematerialized) once it refreshed its audience-scoped effective authority (D950). A refresh that advances past the receiver's known history (a Mission it holds no row for, or a version above the stored one) raises the latch, or advances an open latch's marker, to the observed version, since the events it skipped may have narrowed authority: accepting newer state does not establish newer authority, so the lease waits for an acknowledgement covering that version (#1824 review). A version gap holds across later events, contiguous ones included, until Status covers it, and also latches rematerialization, since the missing event may have narrowed authority; a Mission released after a restore is latched at the released version. A row a store wrote before the observation columns gives no lease until a Status refresh

requirements.notes: A restart on the declared file-backed single-writer store keeps the state version and the terminal tombstone, so no lower version is served after recovery and the committed-but-unpublished transition replays at its own version. With a recovery witness configured (#250 step 3, slice A), the kernel holds its store and its witness's lock exclusively (so a copied store cannot share the witness), and opens only when the store's recovery marker matches the witness, a file outside the database restore unit that every write transaction advances (intent before the commit, finalized after it): a restored older store, a lost, unreadable or foreign witness and an unresolved intent refuse to open, a witnessed store refuses to open without its witness, and a run-time witness or commit failure, a witness changed underneath it, or a write that bypassed the guard (every statement API that can write is guarded), stops every further write and is recorded in the witness, so a restart refuses until reconciled. Offline reconciliation under both locks acknowledges or abandons an intent, or accepts a store with a recorded uncertainty under a new generation, and never lowers the witness. The Authorization Server builds only on an admitted store (a shipped launcher requires the witness with MISSION_KERNEL_STORE, and `pnpm as-native` refuses to start on a restored older store), and while a running kernel is uncertain it answers every request but discovery metadata and the key set with 503 temporarily_unavailable, a request already in flight included (the release fence checks again after every await). The transaction inventory (control-plane-deployment.md) names every kernel table and how its writes are witnessed, and a test fails on a table it does not name. Not yet covered: a way back from an older store other than restoring the witnessed one, by invalidating authority under a new generation (slice B); and any topology beyond one writer on one host. The escape detector notices a bypassing write only at the next guarded transaction, after that write committed. No waiver of existing binding-level requirements. The retaining consumer's high-water obligation is its own row, control-plane.consistency.rollback-retaining-consumer.

requirements.text: A retaining consumer MUST key its high-water mark by the canonical (issuer, mission_id) tuple, reject a lower version, and retain the high-water mark across its own recovery.

observation.normative: a retaining consumer keys its high-water mark by (issuer, mission_id), rejects an event at a lower version, and keeps the high-water mark across its own recovery
observation.local: the Signals receiver (#1323) keys its state by (issuer, audience, mission_id), finer than the tuple, and keeps it in the consumer's store across a restart. A SET with a fresh jti at an equal or lower version is answered stale, before and after a restart; a redelivery of a SET whose jti it has seen is answered duplicate, before and after a restart; and the same Mission identifier at another issuer keeps its own sequence. With a recovery witness (#1749), a file outside the store's directory tree advanced before every commit, a store restored from an older backup or replaced by an empty one is detected when the receiver opens: every Mission, retained or not, is held (no event applied or recorded, no lease, no view) until a Mission Status response to a nonce the receiver issued under the current recovery generation verifies and reports a version no lower than the store's, and that state, the high-water mark and the release commit in one transaction. The response must also be inside its reliance bound (its fresh_until, exp, and for an active Mission its expires_at). One witnessed writer: the witness's lock is held while the receiver is open, the store records the witness's path, the witness is read back before every write, and a store this receiver witnesses refuses an unwitnessed open. An outbox or equivalent satisfies this only when it shares the state transaction. A second Signals database does not join that transaction merely because its API is called inside it. Publication can duplicate, reorder, or stop after commit: event identity and Mission/version correlation make redelivery idempotent and gaps detectable, and consumers resynchronize from an authoritative state surface. Non-active transitions receive priority. The profile does not promise global delivery order or require a particular worker/claiming topology.

requirements.notes: Every commit funnel writes an immutable event row with an in-transaction event identity on the kernel handle, in the state write's own transaction, and publishes only after that commit; a rollback leaves no event, delivery row or tombstone. A publication lost after commit replays the persisted payload with the same identity and commit timestamp, so the Signals SET carries one jti across redelivery and its unique event key makes the replay a no-op. Durable retryable subscribers are acknowledged independently with bounded backoff, and a removed subscriber's pending row reaches a terminal disposition without blocking others. Delivery is at least once with idempotent acceptance: exactly-once external delivery is not claimed, and multi-process claiming and worker topology stay under #641's trigger. The one subscriber whose effect leaves the process, the per-delegation family grant revocation, is captured in the terminal transaction and awaited by the request-path drain, replacing a fire-and-forget promise with a swallowed rejection. The committing caller still learns that publication did not complete, while the recovery path isolates an unpublishable event so one poison row cannot fail a request that committed nothing. Overlapping drains are serialized on the outbox instance: one pass runs at a time, a caller arriving mid-pass joins one follow-up pass that starts after it, and every disposition write is guarded on the pending row and on the attempt that produced it, so a terminal disposition never moves and a stale attempt never rewrites the attempt count, the error or the backoff. The controlled-promise cases cover both completion orders, the recorded attempt counts, the request-path seam under four concurrent drains, and the follow-up pass that keeps a row enqueued mid-pass live; the two-instance cases exercise the interleaving serialization removes, in one process over one handle and with no lease. Multi-process claiming and fencing stay under #641's trigger.

requirements.text: Before each activation, the activating issuer MUST compute `digest` over the exact snapshot it evaluates, and MUST NOT activate the instance under that policy when the result differs

observation.normative: an activation under a policy snapshot whose digest differs from the committed digest does not activate under that policy: Template refuses with dispatch_policy_changed, Progressive falls back to a fresh human approval, Child Delegation denies with policy_denied
observation.local: Template: a held snapshot edited under the same version, a changed version, or no snapshot refuses dispatch_policy_changed with no instance and no dispatch row committed; the committed snapshot still dispatches. The Agent selection rule is read only from the verified snapshot (its `select_agent` member), so a rule re-pointed under the same version refuses dispatch_policy_changed and never selects. Child Delegation: the same three changes deny policy_denied (with deny Child Evidence) and commit no child; restoring the snapshot admits creation. Eligibility reads only the current registry: a policy replaced under a new version, edited under the same version, or retired refuses even while its exact committed snapshot is retained for audit, and the refusal retains nothing for the changed bytes. Progressive: a drawdown policy edited under an unchanged version falls back to the deferred fresh approval and creates no successor by policy; the committed snapshot restored, the drawdown is adjudicated. All three clauses are asserted.

requirements.text: The issuer MUST retain each snapshot's bytes and media type for the audit horizon

observation.normative: the snapshot bytes and media type behind each activation policy digest are retained for the audit horizon of every Mission activated under that snapshot, so the digest reproduces
observation.local: Template and Child Delegation: every successful Dispatch and policy-adjudicated child creation retains the snapshot its gate verified (for a child, every justifying entry's child_creation_policy), keyed by (issuer, policy id, version, digest), with the exact bytes, the media type and the anchor's typ and iss, on the kernel database inside the record's own transaction: a retention failure commits no Mission, dispatch row or reservation. A write recomputes the digest and refuses bytes that do not reproduce it, never rewrites retained bytes, and only moves the horizon forward. The horizon is the latest expires_at of a Mission activated under the snapshot plus the declared audit retention (7776000 seconds, the value the terminal tombstones compose); boot recovery prunes only rows past it, and replacing, editing or retiring a policy in the registry deletes nothing. An auditor recomputes an old activation's committed digest from the retained row after the registry changes; an unretained or pruned commitment reports unavailable and a tampered row mismatch. Durable only on the file-backed kernel store (restart witnessed); the in-memory default does not survive a restart. Unit witnesses only, below the row's endpoint level. Progressive: a policy-adjudicated drawdown retains its verified drawdown policy snapshot in the creation transaction, and the successor's commitment verifies from it (endpoint witness, #1017).

The gate call at commit has no failing input to refuse (the record builder emits only records the gate admits), so the gate is witnessed as a function on variants of a committed record, as for governed_policy. observation.local: Witnessed for the governed_policy accountable assertion: the deciding policy is the root or the evaluator the root commits, and an unauthorized approving human yields no consent and no activation. A human's eligibility under approval_policy is exercised on recorded direct approvals (the direct approval rule's authority-source activators, Subjects, approve-for and write eligibility, #1470 slice 1); service eligibility is not exercised. A contributing policy assertion is authorized on recorded ceiling drawdowns (#1470 slice 2): the drawdown policy must be one the recording rule admits and the one the ceiling consent committed, and the consenting human eligible under the rule's consent eligibility; otherwise the drawdown falls back to a fresh human approval and nothing contributes. That eligibility is a current check backed by the retained authenticated consent: the configuration current at the drawdown's commit, retained with it. It does not reproduce consent-time eligibility (the configuration at consent time is not retained) or consent-time authentication strength. The row stays partial for those specific gaps: service eligibility under approval_policy is not exercised, and a drawdown's consent eligibility is not checked as of consent time.

NOT covered, each by ruling: a token the release fence refuses keeps its count, its Mission having ended (D771, D772); a crash or a lost response after the count is never observed and stays counted, the fail-safe (D772, D874); and a held or replayed reservation keeps its count, since an earlier attempt took it (a Dispatch Handoff redemption that fails inside the handler keeps its reservation for the retry that replays it). requirements.text: the AS SHOULD include, alongside `error`, the `mission_error` token-error-response member

observation.normative: lifecycle refusals carry mission_error with one of revoked, expired, superseded, derivations_exhausted, or a value a companion defines (Mission Status's suspended and completed, Child Delegation's parent_terminated)
observation.local: oidc-provider 9.10's err_out.js copies only error, error_description, scope and state from a thrown error, so MissionGrantError and MissionExchangeError plus a grant.error listener splice mission_error into the body wherever the Mission gate (the refresh pre-check, gateDerivation or gateActive) refuses a still-valid grant. The Token Exchange handlers that write their own refusal body (the async-delegation exchange, its family rollback and recovery, carryover retrieval, child-creation recovery, and the expansion predecessor and recovery checks) add it from the refused Mission's observed record, after client authentication and possession (#1179). The rollback stores the member with the refusal, so a replay to the same client and key repeats it. Possession of a Mission's token does not authorize the presenter, so the expansion predecessor check, expansion recovery and child-creation recovery name the Mission's state only to the predecessor's or parent's own client, the acting agent this deployment authorizes; an unrelated client holding the token and its key gets the refusal without it. Since #1326 the step-4 acting-client check refuses such a client earlier, before the creation lookup on both exchanges and before redeem at the deferred poll, so these three client gates are unreachable at the endpoint and stay as defense in depth; the cross-client expansion test now witnesses that the earlier refusal carries no mission_error. Child-creation recovery also requires the presented token's authority, actor and depth to admit the recorded child; a narrower token from the same client and key gets the same invalid_request without the state. These disclosure tests are local choices. Endpoint witnesses cited here: suspended on a refresh (tracer); derivations_exhausted on a capped Mission's second derivation (tracer) and on the async-delegation family rollback; superseded on a refresh of a predecessor's own refresh token after a deferred expansion activated its successor, with nothing issued, saved or counted (refresh-precheck, #1065), and on a new expansion of that superseded predecessor; expired on a Token Exchange, whose lifecycle refusal is invalid_request (#1154); suspended and revoked on the async-delegation exchange, its recovery, carryover retrieval, child-creation recovery, the expansion predecessor check and expansion recovery, and revoked on the family rollback and its replay; and parent_terminated on child-creation recovery after the parent's revocation (#1179). The shared mapper gateErrorToMissionError, which passes each termination reason through (superseded, parent_terminated, expired) and gives no value for an unrecognized one, is cited as a unit witness, not as an endpoint refusal. Partial: completed is not cited here as an endpoint refusal. This demo's own /lifecycle route destroys the underlying OAuth Grant on a terminal transition (provider.ts), so a refresh after it fails at oidc-provider's grant lookup with no mission_error; a raw kernel transition, natural expiry or supersession leaves the grant for the Mission gate.

requirements.text: A Mission Issuer MUST accept, through an authenticated means independent of possession of any token, a revocation by `mission_id` from a party the deployment's policy authorizes

observation.normative: a party the deployment's policy authorizes to revoke the Mission, authenticated through a means independent of possession of any token, revokes it by its `mission_id`, after which every derivation under the Mission refuses
observation.local: the token-independent means is the advertised Mission Lifecycle endpoint: a lifecycle client registered with no grant at the token endpoint authenticates by private_key_jwt with its own key, presents no access, refresh or service token, and holds the deployment's configured `mission_lifecycle` authorization. The reference also serves an additional, token-authenticated path, which the requirement neither requires nor forbids: a service principal presenting a service token at the development route, under the same `mission_lifecycle` authorization

requirements.notes: #1182 (D378). #1503 finding 14 (D620): the obligation names a party the deployment's policy authorizes, not the Subject, the Approver or an administrator by role, so the former partial gap (Subject and Approver access to the surface not exercised) no longer describes an obligation; that no role alone authorizes revocation is core.revocation.no-role-entitlement. #1892 ruling 9 (D1026): re-quoted to the Mission Issuer's duty; the observation follows the text's "independent of possession of any token", replacing "holding none of the Mission's tokens", which a token-authenticated path also meets. The two witnesses prove different things. The revoke-only Lifecycle test carries every clause: a security tool registered with no grant at the token endpoint authenticates by private_key_jwt with its own key, presents no token, revokes by mission_id under its configured lifecycle authorization, and the refresh, the family refresh and a new exchange then refuse with nothing saved. The workload-principal test (step 8) authenticates by a service token at the development route: it witnesses an additional, token-authenticated revocation path, used by a party holding none of the Mission's tokens, and the refusals after it, not the token-independent means.

requirements.text: When the AS establishes that the principal identified by a Mission's recorded `subject` ({{record-principal-members}}) has been deprovisioned, it SHOULD terminate that Mission with termination reason `revoked`

observation.normative: when the AS establishes that the principal identified by a Mission's recorded subject (iss, sub) is deprovisioned, every Mission of that Subject not yet terminated, a suspended one included, is terminated with reason revoked and further issuance is refused; temporary disablement, a source outage or an unavailable lookup terminates nothing, nor does the departure or disablement of an Approver, owner or client who is not the recorded Subject; already-issued tokens are not recalled by the termination itself
observation.local: the reference's declared dependency (config/authority-dependencies.json, subject_deprovisioned mapped to revoke): the authorization server's reconciler (services/authorization-server/src/adapters/authority-reconciler.ts) evaluates each governed Mission's recorded subject against the identity source, matched by iss (the source's issuer) and sub, and commits revoke through the lifecycle operation for any Mission not yet terminated, a suspended one included; the Mission Status endpoint then reports it terminated with reason revoked and the issuance gates refuse it. A disabled Subject is suspended, not revoked; a source that cannot be read, or that holds no record of the principal, commits nothing; an Approver's or a client identifier's disablement or deprovisioning changes nothing unless that principal is the recorded Subject

requirements.notes: #1892 ruling 9 (iv) (D1026). Shares its witness with status.lifecycle.rfc7009-not-by-itself, Mission Status's statement of the same rule. The witness revokes, at the RFC 7009 endpoint, the refresh token of an async-delegation family under the Mission (a Token Exchange refresh lineage), asserts the 200 and the family's grant destroyed, and asserts the Mission's state is still active: no transition, for an active Mission. Partial: it runs with the delegation capability on, and no test revokes an access token or a code-redemption refresh token, or a token of a suspended or terminated Mission, and then checks that the Mission's state is unchanged. #1893 review: the observation states no lifecycle transition rather than an active Mission, since a suspended or terminated Mission keeps its state.

requirements.text: Unless the referenced Mission is `active`, the AS MUST refuse a request to derive a token at the token endpoint: a Token Exchange ({{RFC8693}}) with the `invalid_request` error code ({{Section 2.2.2 of RFC8693}}), and any other grant, refresh included, with the `invalid_grant` error code.

observation.normative: a derivation from a Mission that is not `active` issues nothing: a Token Exchange is refused `invalid_request` and a refresh `invalid_grant`, on the explicit state checks and on the save-time gate and lifetime clamp alike
observation.local: Token Exchange witnessed on async delegation (explicit check and lifetime clamp), expansion and child creation; refresh on the async-delegation family; the deferred grant on the AROP poll, pending or approved, and the Mission approval poll, each with the Mission's own mission_error and the deferral left pollable after a resume; and the AROP deferral initiation by the Mission's own client on a revoked, expired or suspended Mission, with no mission_error, since the initiation presents no Mission grant (D863), opening no deferral, issuing no token and counting no derivation, with the same initiation opening one after a resume (#1740, D862). Another client, or any client naming an unknown Mission, gets the indistinguishable invalid_request before the state check, and an unauthenticated client invalid_client first, each with no mission_error, no deferral, no token and no derivation counted; those witnesses in the same describe are regression witnesses of the reference's disclosure choice and are not cited. The authorization-code and JWT-bearer paths keep invalid_grant through the same refusal mapping, pinned by its unit test.

requirements.notes: #1154 (D369). Deferred polls aligned to invalid_grant (#250). #1740 (D862, D863): the AROP deferral initiation answered its own client invalid_request for a Mission that is not active; it answers invalid_grant, with no mission_error. Mutation-proved: answering it invalid_request again (the handleDeferredGrant catch in adapters/provider.ts) fails every cited initiation witness and the D859 separation witness; adding the Mission's mission_error to that refusal (the pre-D863 lifecycleMissionError argument, from the expiry-applied record) fails the same witnesses on the absent member; reducing the pre-open ownership check to an existence check fails the other-client witnesses (not cited) and the #1348 ownership witness.

requirements.text: The AS MUST refuse a derivation request it answers after it has acknowledged a revocation of the Mission, with the same error code.

observation.normative: after a revocation is acknowledged, a Token Exchange is refused `invalid_request` and any other grant, refresh included, `invalid_grant`, and nothing is issued
observation.local: the reference re-reads Mission state at release (the release fence, #1498), after the save-time gate, the signature and the request-path drain, on every 200 that releases an access token naming a Mission this AS issues, a stored result served again included; it orders a revocation against an issuance within one process only (#641). Every fenced path is witnessed with the fence disabled delivering a token: the code exchange, refresh and the async family's refresh, the device code grant, the deferred grant (AROP, Mission approval and expansion deferrals), the JWT-bearer grant (child and Dispatch Handoff redemption), the Mission dispatch grant, the delegation-handle, async-delegation, designation, delegated-redemption, child-creation, ceiling-drawdown and Dispatch Handoff exchanges, and the async-delegation, expansion and Mission dispatch stored results. A refusal carries mission_error with the released Mission's own termination reason (parent_terminated for a child whose parent was revoked). The ICA continuation exchange answers ICA's codes (core.issuance-gating.profile-code-override) and the transaction endpoint access_denied. Work committed before the fence stays spent: the Dispatch Handoff redemption's counted derivation and consumed grant, the designation and delegated redemption's counted derivation, the AROP and Mission approval deferrals' redemption, and an expansion successor's recorded delivery, which recovery never serves because it refuses the terminated successor first (#250)

requirements.notes: #1795 (D919). The ordered MUST is unchanged (D610, D845). Each step's content has its own rows; this row records the order, at the boundaries an observer of the approval surface can distinguish. An ordering with no observable effect, such as computing the independent expiry ceiling before step 3, is not asserted here, and the MUST still governs it. #1802: two of the three boundaries have witnesses. The first (an Approver whose authentication fails, or who may not activate the source, is refused before step 5 renders and is shown nothing of it) is witnessed at the approval page on the browser, device, headless and upstream-login paths, including a login that ages out during the page's last await and a refusal whose description would otherwise name the request. The expiry boundary is witnessed by the two decision tests in which the requested expiry passes before or during the commit, each creating no Mission, grant or code. The failed-commit boundary (no active Mission and no usable Mission-bound grant after a failed commit) has browser-path witnesses since #1863, which commits at the code save: a code-storage failure (both kernels), a refused commit and a lapsed hold each leave no Mission and no redeemable code, and a held grant whose commit was refused and whose deletion failed is not reused and refuses a token mint. A recovery-witness failure releases no code but can leave the record durable under an uncertain kernel, so it is not cited for no active Mission. On the device path, where a profile-defined grant (the device code) exists while the request is pending, a refused commit leaves no Mission and the device code polls access_denied, and a grant-store failure before the commit leaves the session pending; each was proved by a mutation on this boundary, activating the device code before the commit or after a refused one (each then fails on its boundary assertion, invalid_grant where authorization_pending or access_denied is expected). Coverage review (D1016): every boundary is witnessed on each implemented path, so the row is tested. Recovery-witness uncertainty and an unrecognized post-commit exception are not cited here: in both the commit itself succeeded (record-code-atomicity carries them). Each render-time witness was proved by disabling its guard alone.

observation.local: decide() prepares the approval (every refusal before any write, except the commit's revalidation of the authority source and of a consented ceiling's drawdown policy, which refuses at the code save), reserves the approval event, classifies the interaction-derived grant as a held approval grant before its first save (append-only: refusal, hold expiry and failed cleanup never make it an ordinary grant), saves the grant, re-checks the context (#1446) and holds the decision, keyed by the grant, until the interaction expires. The provider's AuthorizationCode adapter fences a code under a held grant: it joins the approval event's serialization, stages the code (stored, not redeemable), then in one synchronous turn runs the final checks (the #1446 context re-check and the approval-authentication floor) and kernel.approve, which commits the record already bound to the grant (a retry's bindGrant is compare-and-set), and releases the code; find returns an unreleased code under a held grant as absent. An IntentError completes access_denied; recovery-witness uncertainty releases nothing; another post-commit failure releases only when the committed record is the held decision. In-process, under the single-process fence (D663): no store spans the kernel and the provider. The device flow commits at its decision (#1202).

requirements.notes: Partial as the settled disposition (coverage review, D1016): atomic for every outcome the fence recognizes, and short of the clause only in two fail-closed exceptional paths, each leaving an active Mission with no usable code: recovery-witness uncertainty after a durable commit (the kernel then refuses every state-dependent service until reconciliation), and an unrecognized post-commit exception (the owner's #1878 choice; reachable only through a defect). A file-backed crash after the commit reaches the accepted delivery gap's end state (D1001). Closing the remainder needs a kernel-backed provider adapter, which the #1863 feasibility answer found buys only a code redeemable after a restart; no further work is planned. #1863 moves the commit from the decision to the code save. Witnessed (approval-code-atomicity.test.ts; both kernels where named): no Mission exists after the decision, and the code save commits the record bound to the grant, whose code redeems under it; a real code-storage failure commits nothing (no Mission, binding, index entry or redeemable code, and the grant stays classified); a refused commit completes access_denied with nothing created; a recovery-witness failure at the commit (file-backed) releases no code, even one whose deletion failed; a notification failure after the commit is recovered and its notification retried; a lapsed hold is refused; a held grant whose commit was refused and whose deletion failed is not reused by an ordinary request on the same session and refuses a token mint; a decision racing the resume is ordered against it, ending with one record and one binding; the commit re-checks the rendered context (approval-context-changes.test.ts) and the approval-authentication floor at its own instant; the code is clamped to the expires_at its commit establishes, again against the hold the code save reads. The #916 witnesses still hold: repeated and concurrent decisions keep one grant and binding, a decision by another Approver, Subject or client is refused before the grant is touched, and the commit revalidates the prepared source. Residuals: on the file-backed kernel a crash after the commit keeps the active Mission and loses its code with provider memory, the end state of the delivery gap (control-plane-deployment.md); the delivery gap itself, a code whose redirect is lost, is bounded by the code's 60 s lifetime clamped to expires_at (provider-integration-port.md section 3.4; code reading, no test). After a recovery-witness failure the record may be durable with the kernel uncertain, and every later write and state-dependent service refuses until reconciliation. Post-commit recovery is typed (#1878 review): a code is released after a commit only on a LifecycleNotificationError or a BoundGrantIndexWriteError, with the record agreeing with the held decision. An unrecognized post-commit exception releases nothing (witnessed), so the Mission it committed has no usable code until expiry or a revocation; a failed index write is recovered (witnessed).

observation.local: config/approval-floor.json is the published statement, documented in config/README.md and read at boot by the strict loader loadApprovalFloor as APPROVAL_FLOOR, which is the AS's floor (buildAuthorizationServer uses opts.approvalFloor ?? APPROVAL_FLOOR). Its deployment_scope is every Mission the AS approves through its approval interaction; its high-risk-authority floor covers irreversible_action, external_commitment and privileged_administration with a browser Approver, accepted acr mfa and a 300 second age bound. With the opt-in standing-payment-dispatch capability off, as shipped, the AS admits no consumption bound (derive refuses every constraint key outside SUPPORTED_CONSTRAINT_KEYS, and PAR refuses max_budget), so the three action kinds are the high-risk kinds it can admit; with it on, a standing-payment instance's Intent carries max_budget, admitted only on dispatch intake under a template consent at the floor and committed with the consumption_bound class-named exception (#813, #1712). The binding requires no serialization, so the AS serves no endpoint or metadata member for the statement; publication is the deployment document. The loader refuses a statement with no or an empty deployment_scope and one with no floors, so the AS does not start without a published floor.

observation.local: the achieved context (acr, auth_time) comes from the authenticated approval surface: a trusted browser login's recorded context (on the as-native target, the acr and auth_time of the ID Token the approval surface's upstream OpenID Connect login validated, #1320) or a headless approval service's registration, never decide()'s body, which refuses identity members. oidc-provider accepts acr_values and max_age only with openid (lib/actions/authorization/check_openid_scope.js, 9.10.0), and openid is available only to a self-approval in this user agent (#826), so a client-requested strength is exercised on self-approvals; an approval for another principal cannot request one here: PAR refuses acr_values or max_age without openid invalid_request, before any interaction (the accepted fail-closed limitation, D305: unsupported, never ignored or downgraded). The published floor (config/approval-floor.json, evaluateApprovalFloor) is evaluated after derivation over the complete derived Authority Set and before any Mission, Grant or code: every action is classified through the AS-owned classification (an unclassified one refuses), and payment execution and remittance invoke the high-risk-authority floor, satisfied only by a browser Approver with achieved acr mfa authenticated at most 300 seconds earlier; a headless service registration never satisfies it. oidc-provider's own check_max_age middleware translates a literal max_age=0 to prompt=login and clears params.max_age before this handler runs, so the implementation recovers that signal from prompt=login (forceFreshLogin) rather than reading a cleared max_age. Where the deployment selects Progressive authorization, the authority ceiling the approval decision consents is validated and classified with the derived set before any write (#1255): a later drawdown grants the ceiling's authority under this consent's consent_principal and approved_at with no Approver authenticating, so a ceiling that admits high-risk authority needs the same floor-meeting Approver, and a refusal leaves no Mission, Grant or code. #1802: step 1 runs before the approval page renders anything: after derivation the page checks the requested acr_values and max_age and the floor over the derived set against the same trusted context, and a login that falls short gets a 401 step-up notice (insufficient_user_authentication) carrying nothing of the request and no render revision; a ceiling the page offers is classified with the derived set and offered only to a login that meets the floor over both. The decision checks both again, so a login that ages out after the rendering is refused there.

requirements.notes: The floor clause binds a high-risk Mission (applicability has no kind for that condition, so the row stays unconditional). D425: the shipped high-risk actions are all write-bearing, so they need a distinct Approver (D37) and a delegated request cannot carry acr_values (D305); the floor/request conjunction is therefore witnessed on an AS whose floor policy classifies invoice.read as high-risk, in both directions. The AS admits no consumption bound (derive refuses every constraint key outside SUPPORTED_CONSTRAINT_KEYS), so none can invoke the floor. An Expansion deferral approval (ExpansionDeferralStore.approve, in process) meets the same floor over the successor's derived authority, from the browser login the trusted approval integration records (ExpansionApproval.authentication); without one a high-risk expansion approval refuses and the deferral stays pending. Each guard (the decide-time and expansion-approval checks, fail-closed and whole-set classification, the headless refusal, acr, age, future and malformed context, conjunctive floors) was disabled in turn and its suite failed. Adopted #636 acceptance criterion (approver-vs-subject tests). The requested-strength cases run on self-approvals in a trusted browser session (#826: a delegated request cannot carry acr_values without openid here); the split-principal case moved to no-token-claim-carriage and openid-refused-when-approver-not-subject. The Deferred Mission Approval companion ({{I-D.draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-approval}} {{deferred-approval}}) that would relocate this same check to an asynchronous reviewer has no reference implementation in src/ (only the unrelated AROP post-Mission-widening deferral is implemented, a different mechanism, {{I-D.ietf-oauth-deferred-token-response}}); a deferred-review wire test is not implementable in this stack and is disclosed here rather than fabricated. A client registration's incompatible OIDC defaults fail closed (#826): `default_acr_values` is invalid client metadata in this deployment, which configures no acr values, so every request from such a client is refused before any interaction; `default_max_age` and `require_auth_time` require `openid`, and with it a delegated approval refuses `invalid_scope`. The `claims` parameter is unsupported (`claims_parameter_supported` false): a request carrying an essential `acr` is served without essential-claim treatment, a disclosed limitation witnessed by "does not support the claims parameter: discovery says so, and a request carrying an essential acr gets no essential-claim treatment (a disclosed limitation)", not by this row. The Mission Device Authorization approval (#1202) runs the same decision, so the floor holds there too: a high-risk device approval by a password Approver creates no Mission and ends the session denied, an mfa one approves; proved by not applying the floor's refusal. #1320 (D496): on the as-native target the browser login is an OpenID Connect login at an upstream provider that authenticates the Approver (a password, then a one-time code its device receives; mfa only after both). The AS validates the ID Token (OpenID Connect Core 1.0 Section 3.1.3.7), maps the issuer-qualified identity to the local Approver and records the token's acr and auth_time, which the floor evaluates unchanged: a password-only login and one older than 300 s at the decision are refused before any Mission or code, at the AS and on the assembled target, and an mfa login is admitted. Proved by recording acr from configuration, stamping auth_time at the callback, and disabling the floor's acr and age checks; the ID Token checks themselves witness no clause of this row and are cited in the deployment documents. #1255: the ceiling witnesses were proved by evaluating the floor over the derived set alone (the password Approver's ceiling was approved), by moving the ceiling's floor check after the grant save (only the zero-Grant assertion failed) and after the Mission commit (the zero-Mission assertion failed), and by refusing every ceiling that admits floor-class authority whatever the Approver (the mfa approval failed). #1802: the render-time checks were proved by dropping the floor from the step-up condition (ten renders returned 200), dropping the requested strength from it (four), and always offering the ceiling (the password page showed it); the decision-time checks by disabling the decision's floor branch (eight approval-floor tests, the two aged-at-the-decision witnesses among them) and its requested-strength check (the max_age aged-at-the-decision witness and both rar-carriage refusals). The former ceiling witness for a password Approver is replaced: that login is no longer offered the ceiling, so its consent is refused as one the page did not render, and the decision's floor over a consented ceiling is witnessed by a login that ages past the bound after the rendering. #1863 (#1878 review): a held browser decision measures both again at its commit, when its authorization code is saved: the floor, and the client's acr_values and max_age (max_age=0 through its prompt=login translation). A login that no longer satisfies either completes access_denied with no Mission and no released code; a within-age control commits and redeems.

requirements.notes: #826. The provider account and grant are the Approver's, logged in with the achieved acr and authentication time; a browser approval keeps that session, and a headless approval leaves the client's user agent none (the resume runs without the user agent's session cookie, the session its login created is destroyed before the response is flushed and its cookie removed, and the code is not session-bound). Mission-bound tokens carry the Subject through the JWT customizer, refresh introspection reports the Subject. Discriminating witnesses: the session and grant belong to Bob and the token sub is Alice (delegated browser approval); a headless approval's resume session no longer exists and no session cookie reaches the user agent; and an earlier Alice session in the same user agent is neither replaced nor renewed. Two clauses hold in this assembly by construction as well: Mission access tokens are resource-audienced, so UserInfo refuses them, and every Mission authorization request needs its own approval interaction, so a prompt=none request is never satisfied silently; their tests assert the outcome, not that the defect alone would have changed it.

requirements.text: an AS MUST NOT derive Mission-bound authority from a client-supplied `mission_id`

observation.normative: a client-supplied mission_id cannot select or alter the Mission used for derivation; if the request is accepted, the emitted Mission is the grant-bound Mission (rejecting the unexpected parameter also conforms)

requirements.text: A Mission MAY carry zero or more grant bindings.

observation.normative: one Mission can carry more than one bound grant lineage at once, for example an authorization-code lineage's refresh-token family and a second refresh-token family a continuation transport establishes later for the same Mission: both resolve to the same Mission id and issuer, and establishing or using the second family neither alters nor supersedes the first family's binding

requirements.text: The AS MUST resolve a bound grant lineage to the same Mission on every derivation performed against it

observation.normative: repeated derivations against one grant lineage (a refresh, or a further Token-Exchange-created family rooted in it) always resolve to, and every issued token's `mission` claim always names, the same Mission id and issuer; no sequence of otherwise-valid requests against that lineage ever changes which Mission it resolves to. No profile-defined operation lets a client present an input naming a different Mission for an already-bound lineage, so a reassignment is an AS-internal storage fault (fail closed, audit), never a client-triggerable, wire-observable refusal

requirements.text: A Token Exchange derivation ({{RFC8693}}) that returns only an access token establishes no new grant lineage

observation.normative: an access-token-only Token Exchange derivation from a Mission-bound `subject_token` (delegation, {{delegation}}, or self-exchange down-scoping, {{self-exchange}}) creates no new grant binding; the issued token is a derived token whose `mission` claim identifies the one Mission its subject_token resolved to. Only a Token Exchange that establishes a redeemable grant lineage (a new refresh-token family, for example the continuation profile's delegation-family-creating exchange, {{I-D.draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-continuation}}) creates a new grant binding, rooted in that same Mission

requirements.text: Where the `subject_token` was issued under a grant lineage, the issued token retains that grant provenance, and a later redemption of a designation derived from it validates all applicable backing-grant state

observation.normative: a token issued by an access-token-only Token Exchange whose subject_token was issued under a grant lineage keeps that lineage: once that lineage is revoked, a designation derived from the issued token is no longer redeemable, whether the issued token is a self-exchanged token or a delegated token
observation.local: Observed through redemption, the one later derivation the OAuth binding names. The self-exchanged token is the reference's delegation handle, whose own provider Grant records the presented token's grant as its backing grant.
